    tidygenclust

    tidygenclust provides functions and methods to run genetic clustering in R, and to align and compare multiple runs of the same or different K. tidygenclust builds on tidypopgen, enhancing the grammar of population genetics with a focus on genetic clustering.

    Its core functionality is native, and needs neither Python nor Julia:

    • gt_radmix(), to estimate ancestry proportions with the ADMIXTURE method, using a modified version of the algorithm of OpenADMIXTURE (Ko et al. 2023), ported to C++ from OpenADMIXTURE.jl;
    • gt_clumppling(), to align multiple clustering runs within and across K with the method of clumppling (Liu, Kopelman & Rosenberg 2024), ported to R and C++, with modifications, from the python package clumppling.

    Optionally, tidygenclust can also run the python packages fastmixture (gt_fastmixture()) and ADAMIXTURE (gt_adamixture()), and the original ADMIXTURE program (tidypopgen::gt_admixture()), which it installs in a conda environment on request.

    Installation

    You can install the development version of tidygenclust from GitHub with:

    # install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("EvolEcolGroup/tidygenclust")

    gt_radmix() and gt_clumppling() work straight away. The optional tools (fastmixture, ADMIXTURE and ADAMIXTURE) are installed with reticulate in a conda environment, ctidygenclust, when you ask for them (this only works on Linux at the moment: on Windows, you can use them through the WSL; on macOS, they are not available, as their OpenMP library conflicts with that of R):

    # all the tools
tgc_tools_install()
# or only some of them
tgc_tools_install(tools = "fastmixture")
# add a tool to an existing environment
tgc_admixture_install()
# check what is installed
tgc_tools_version()

    Overview of functionality

    An overview of the functionality of tidygenclust and its integration with tidypopgen is provided in the “Get Started” vignette. This also includes a detailed description of how to align multiple runs of clustering and compare them. The article “Installing and running external tools” shows how to install and run the optional external programs.

    Clumppling

    gt_clumppling() aligns the runs stored in a gt_admix object (created by any of the clustering functions, or read from Q files with tidypopgen::read_q_files()), detects modes among runs with the same K, and aligns the modes across K, with the method of clumppling (Liu, Kopelman & Rosenberg 2024). Its code is ported, with modifications, from the python package clumppling (version 2.0.10, by Xiran Liu), and we are grateful to its authors; if you use it, please cite Liu, Kopelman & Rosenberg (2024). It reproduces the results of clumppling 2.0.10, against which the test suite checks it, and it is much faster (about 0.1 seconds, rather than about 9 seconds with python, for the 200 runs of the capeverde example):

    capeverde <- readRDS(
  system.file("extdata", "capeverde_admix.rds", package = "tidygenclust")
)
# the Cape Verde example of clumppling (Verdu et al. 2017)
clump_res <- gt_clumppling(capeverde, seed = 1)
autoplot(clump_res, type = "modes", group = capeverde$group)

    See data-raw/clumppling/README.md for details of the port.

    Ancestry estimation with gt_radmix()

    gt_radmix() estimates individual ancestry proportions (Q) and ancestral allele frequencies (P) with the ADMIXTURE method (Alexander et al. 2009), using a modified version of the fast algorithm of OpenADMIXTURE (Ko et al. 2023). Much of its C++ (OpenMP) code is ported from OpenADMIXTURE.jl, and we are grateful to its authors. It has a different name because it differs from OpenADMIXTURE: it does not include the selection of ancestry informative markers that is part of OpenADMIXTURE; we implemented the cross-validation of ADMIXTURE, to choose K, which is not part of OpenADMIXTURE; it supports pseudohaploid data; and it changes some details of the computations (see ?gt_radmix). If you use it, please cite Ko et al. (2023) for the algorithm, as well as Alexander et al. (2009) for the method. It needs neither Python nor Julia: genotypes are read directly from the backing file of a gen_tibble, and results are returned as gt_admix objects, which work with all the methods of tidypopgen and with gt_clumppling(). Cross-validation, as in ADMIXTURE, is computed with crossval = TRUE.

    adm <- gt_radmix(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, seed = c(1, 2, 3),
                 crossval = TRUE, n_cores = 4)
autoplot(adm, type = "cv")

    Apart from the documented changes, it reproduces the computations of OpenADMIXTURE.jl to numerical precision, and it agrees with ADMIXTURE 1.3.0, which the test suite checks against stored results; on the 379 individuals and 54,051 SNPs of the EUR_subset data used to test OpenADMIXTURE.jl, it is 2-3 times faster than ADMIXTURE on a single thread, and about 10 times faster on 4 threads. See ?gt_radmix, the article “Benchmarking gt_radmix() against ADMIXTURE, fastmixture and ADAMIXTURE” (in the Articles section of the website of the package), and data-raw/radmix/README.md for details.

    References

    Alexander DH, Novembre J, Lange K (2009) Fast model-based estimation of ancestry in unrelated individuals. Genome Research, 19(9), 1655-1664.

    Ko S, Chu BB, Peterson D, Okenwa C, Papp JC, Alexander DH, Sobel EM, Zhou H, Lange KL (2023) Unsupervised discovery of ancestry informative markers and genetic admixture proportions in biobank-scale datasets. The American Journal of Human Genetics, 110(2), 314-325.

    Liu X, Kopelman NM, Rosenberg NA (2024) Clumppling: cluster matching and permutation program with integer linear programming. Bioinformatics, 40(1), btad751.

    Verdu P, Jewett EM, Pemberton TJ, Rosenberg NA, Baptista M (2017) Parallel trajectories of genetic and linguistic admixture in a genetically admixed creole population. Current Biology, 27(16), 2529-2535.
